title: Dealing with Diminishers
hook: Roger Fisher and William Ury keep interests ahead of positions before status eats the answer.
counterintuition: Under a Diminisher, the first useful move is smaller than victory: decide what you can still influence. Silence and head-on fights both miss that middle space.
tryThisNow: Mark one sentence in a current request where you are trying to win a position. Then rewrite it as a how-question about the interest or risk you need heard.
keyTakeaway: When a Diminisher has more power, split control from influence: move from positions to interests, ask how constraints will be handled, and keep useful risk visible.

breakdown.fastRead:
Roger Fisher keeps the useful answer alive by shifting the exchange from position to interest.

Getting to Yes, the frame linked with Fisher and William Ury, gives one side: do not turn pressure into a status fight. A Diminisher's control leaves less thought visible.

The 2017 sequence adds dealing with Diminishers, so you may be under the power, not holding it. You cannot control a boss's personality. You can influence frame, evidence, and request.

Amy Edmondson's voice-and-silence work gives the counterweight: quiet can hide risk. Neither defiance nor blank compliance is the aim. Ask what problem must be solved, whose constraint matters, and how risk gets heard.
breakdown.deepRead:
The move works because it changes the first question. Instead of asking how to beat this person, you ask what interest is buried under the position. An interest is the need under a demand. A position is the demand stated as fixed.

Use this only where a reply can protect facts or ownership. If speaking would bring serious personal risk, get help outside the exchange. If the choice is already yours to obey, do not dress delay up as courage. The tactic has a cost.

Getting to Yes gives the problem side. Roger Fisher and William Ury's frame separates people from the problem, which means you stop making personality the whole case. Their useful contrast is interests not positions. That does not excuse harsh conduct. It gives you a usable target: the constraint, the evidence, or the request.

Chris Voss, a former FBI negotiator, adds the question side. A calibrated question is a shaped prompt, often built around how, that pulls the other person into the constraint. How should I handle the deadline with the missing facts? How do you want ownership split if the risk remains? The question is not surrender. It makes control answer to reality.

Amy Edmondson's psychological safety work, about whether people feel able to speak up, stops the tactic from becoming quiet obedience. Silence can look smooth while risk goes underground. A useful response keeps intelligence visible without forcing every concern into a fight.

So carry the contrast. Positions harden; interests give you something to solve. Silence soothes; voice keeps risk in view. Keep the problem on the table.
breakdown.fullRead:
Roger Fisher and William Ury pull you away from the status fight. Amy Edmondson pulls you away from false calm. The revised 2017 placement needs both. Without the first, dealing with a Diminisher becomes a dare. Without the second, it becomes a quiet loss.

The Fisher-Ury side starts with a plain split. Interests are the needs that explain why a demand matters. Positions are the fixed claims people defend once status enters. If a Diminisher says the answer is final, matching force with force may only feed the contest. The better first question is sharper: What can you influence before status eats the facts?

This is where separating people from the problem matters. You may have strong feelings about the person. You may even be right. But a diagnosis of personality often gives you no handle. The problem might give you one: missing evidence, unclear ownership, a constraint no one has named, or a request that can be made smaller.

Chris Voss belongs on this side of the contrast, not as a third pole. His calibrated questions give the sentence shape for the same move. A how-question can make the constraint part of the exchange. It asks the Diminisher to engage with the task instead of only asserting control. That can be useful when direct defiance would tighten the grip.

Then Edmondson changes the guardrail. Psychological safety means people feel able to speak up; the warning here is that silence can hide risk. If your tactic teaches you to stay quiet forever, it has failed. The price of blank compliance is hidden risk with your name still near it.

So the move is not be nicer and hope. It is not fight harder and call that courage. It is a narrower craft: split control from influence, carry evidence into the exchange, ask about ownership with care, and surface risk in the least reckless form you can find.

You can run this without rank. In a shared project, mark the line where you are trying to win a position. Rewrite it as the interest you need heard. If the other person has more power, ask how the constraint should be handled. If the answer goes quiet, ask what risk is now hidden by the quiet.

The order matters. Start with what you can influence, or you waste energy trying to remake the Diminisher's personality. Use questions, or you may trigger a control contest before the facts are visible. Surface risk, or you may buy short peace with long damage.

This is not permission to endure anything. Some settings need exit, formal help, or a clear no. Some issues deserve direct challenge. The promise is smaller and more useful: before you choose silence or collision, test the space where framing, evidence, and a careful request can keep contribution alive.

Keep the problem on the table.

examples.title: The Harder Position

planSpec.requiredBeat: return moment skips the shift from position to interest

examples.scenario: At the return point, Roger Fisher and William Ury's Getting to Yes frame has one plain check: did the exchange move from position to interest? It does not. The person under the Diminisher comes back with a tougher counter-position, and interests not positions is skipped. Status wins; the facts that might have solved the problem stay out. A blue mark sits beside the missed interest.
examples.whatToDo: What got skipped? Ask for the interest under the demand before you harden your counter-position. Mark the fact that needs daylight, then use it.
examples.whyItMatters: Who pays? The useful facts do. A stronger position can feel brave while it leaves the problem unsolved. The Diminisher still owns the frame.

examples.title: The Late Separation

planSpec.audience: readers whose diagnosis has become personal
planSpec.stakes: a usable request lost inside character judgment
planSpec.requiredBeat: trace the miss back and catch the separation late

examples.scenario: After the exchange is over, Roger Fisher and William Ury's Getting to Yes explains why it nearly broke. The response had made the Diminisher's personality the whole problem, so every sentence became a trial of character. The late catch was smaller: use interests not positions, separate the person from the problem, then ask which constraint or request still needs an answer. The exchange did not become warm, but it became usable.
examples.whatToDo: What caused the miss? Trace the exchange back to the first personal diagnosis. Move the sentence from character to constraint.
examples.whyItMatters: Why does the late catch matter? It gives you a handle when the personality verdict gives you only heat. Use the handle before the next answer hardens.

examples.title: The Quiet Risk

planSpec.audience: readers tempted to treat quiet as solved
planSpec.stakes: risk hidden from the person who needs it
planSpec.requiredBeat: outside effect appears before the return point is met

examples.scenario: Outside the exchange, Amy Edmondson's psychological safety and speaking up warning lands first on the person who needed the hidden risk. Quiet compliance has been treated as proof that the issue is gone, so no one has heard the missing concern. The call stays silent. The return point is set but not met: the concern must be raised in a safer form before the task can be trusted.
examples.whatToDo: What does skipping this cost? The risk moves out of sight. Mark the concern in the least reckless form you can use, and name who needs to hear it.
examples.whyItMatters: Who feels it first? Often the person who needed the warning, not the one who stayed quiet. Compliance is not the same as solved.

examples.title: The How Question

planSpec.stakes: defiance tightening control before facts appear
planSpec.requiredBeat: early signal is caught by a how-oriented question

examples.scenario: Before anyone flags it, the early signal is a demand that leaves no owner for the constraint. Chris Voss, a former FBI negotiator, gives the tactic that catches it. A how-oriented prompt asks the Diminisher to engage the limit: how should this be handled with the facts still missing? The cost is real. Direct defiance would feel cleaner, but the question earns problem-solving space.
examples.whatToDo: Why does the question work? It makes control answer the constraint. Ask how the Diminisher wants ownership handled before you refuse outright.
examples.whyItMatters: What cost gets paid? You give up the clean rush of defiance. In return, the other side must face the limit, not only assert power.

examples.title: The Safety Standard

planSpec.audience: readers who equate safety with staying quiet
planSpec.requiredBeat: standard is stated and the passivity miss is caught late

examples.scenario: The standard is stated at the start: safety cannot mean never raising a concern. Amy Edmondson's psychological safety and speaking up warning makes the miss visible. The first response heads toward passivity, because quiet feels safer than voice. The concern is rescued when it is reframed as useful information, not as a personal attack, and the risk is surfaced.
examples.whatToDo: What would you ask here? Whether the safer move keeps useful intelligence visible or merely keeps you small. Choose the first.
examples.whyItMatters: What makes the catch barely enough? It turns safety away from passivity before the concern disappears. That is the hard line.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood mediator borrows this negotiation move for a rent dispute. What has to travel with the move?
choices: Tie the move to Getting to Yes and its named authors, Roger Fisher and William Ury, so the frame is traceable.
Use the move because the building owner approves it, letting rank stand in for a source when pressure is high.
Save the source until after the dispute calms down, since naming the frame early may slow the exchange.
questions.explanation: The source lineage matters here. Rank can make a tactic sound approved, but Fisher and Ury make the negotiation frame checkable instead of generic.

questions.prompt: A failed exchange ended with both sides judging character. Which earlier choice caused the slide?
choices: They asked for interests too soon, before the senior person had restated the final position in full.
They trusted a calm tone as proof that the problem had been separated from personal conflict.
They made personality the whole case instead of keeping the problem itself available for action.
questions.explanation: The failure came from letting personality swallow the problem. The calm-tone answer uses the wrong proof; tone alone does not keep the exchange usable.

questions.prompt: A school committee hears no objections after a hard demand. What should the silence suggest?
choices: Silence may be hiding risk, because speaking up can feel costly under authority.
The demand has probably solved the problem, because quiet compliance is the clearest proof.
The concern should wait for a senior sponsor, because only rank can make risk visible.
questions.explanation: Edmondson's warning keeps quiet from becoming proof. The sponsor answer borrows authority, but the real issue is whether risk has gone unseen.

questions.prompt: A mentor wants to teach how-questions under pressure. What keeps the tactic from sounding like jargon?
choices: Present it as a common office habit, since broad labels make the method easier to accept.
Borrow the credibility of whoever has the highest title in the group using the question.
Name Chris Voss and his FBI negotiation experience as the lineage behind the tactic.
questions.explanation: Voss's FBI negotiation background gives the tactic a real source. Calling it a common habit makes it sound easy, but it loses the lineage the fact supplies.

questions.prompt: A lab partner says safety means never raising the concern. What is the best correction?
choices: Let quiet stand until the risk becomes undeniable, because safety should remove all strain from the exchange.
Keep useful information visible while managing risk, so coping does not shrink into passivity.
Make the concern a direct personal challenge, because visible contribution requires open confrontation.
questions.explanation: Coping should protect contribution, not reward permanent quiet. The direct-challenge answer reacts to passivity by overshooting into needless confrontation.

questions.prompt: A tenant facing a controlling landlord sees only submission or exit. What is actually wrong?
choices: The tenant is trying to gather evidence too late, after the chance to shape framing, evidence, and requests has fully disappeared.
The tenant has confused control with influence and missed the space for framing, evidence, and requests.
The tenant needs to change the landlord's personality before any request can matter, because control must come before influence.
questions.explanation: Control and influence have been collapsed into one choice. The personality answer aims at the wrong target; no tactic gives you command over someone else's character.

questions.prompt: A clinic dispute failed after everyone defended a fixed demand. Which missing step explains it?
choices: They named the source tradition but aimed it at the wrong proof, treating citation as settlement.
They separated the people from the problem only after the final demand had already hardened.
They argued positions instead of uncovering the interests that would reveal the problem to solve.
questions.explanation: The fact points to interests rather than positions. Late separation is tempting, but this stem is about fixed demands, so the missing step is the interest layer.

questions.prompt: A reader claims the model is only for people already in charge. Which answer fits the 2017 sequence?
choices: The claim holds if the person under pressure lacks rank, since the model has no response path for that side.
Added material on dealing with Diminishers puts response tactics in scope for people below the power line.
The added topic should be treated as a side note until someone with authority chooses to use it.
questions.explanation: The publisher page places dealing with Diminishers in the revised material. The rank-based answer fails because the added topic serves people under the behavior too.

questions.prompt: A project sponsor imposes a demand and direct refusal may tighten control. What maps from Voss?
choices: Ask a how-oriented question that makes constraints and ownership part of the problem to solve.
Wait until the pressure is gone, then raise the same question after the decision has settled.
Treat a calm answer as enough proof that the sponsor has engaged with the real constraints.
questions.explanation: A calibrated how-question creates problem-solving space without direct defiance. Waiting until the decision settles uses the right question too late.

reviewCards.front: What split starts the response to a Diminisher?
reviewCards.back: Separate control from influence. You cannot make the Diminisher's personality change on command, but you can shape framing, evidence, and requests.

reviewCards.front: What does Getting to Yes add here?
reviewCards.back: It moves you from positions to interests. Instead of arguing harder for a fixed demand, look for the need or constraint that can be solved.

reviewCards.front: Why is quiet compliance not enough proof?
reviewCards.back: Amy Edmondson's voice-and-silence warning says quiet can hide risk when speaking up feels costly. Treat silence as a signal to examine, not a pass.
When direct refusal would tighten control, a how-question asks the other person to face constraints and ownership instead of only asserting control.
It should keep useful intelligence visible while managing risk. If coping trains you to stay quiet forever, it is rewarding passivity.

reviewCards.front: When should you not use the move?
reviewCards.back: Do not use it to pretend you can control someone's personality or to stay in serious personal risk. Use it where framing, evidence, or a request can still matter.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Request
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Mark the Request. Find the line where pressure has turned into a fixed demand, then mark what you can still influence: frame, evidence, or request. The skill is not to win every exchange; it is to keep useful contribution visible without pretending you control the Diminisher.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe a demand stated as final; note the interest or constraint it hides.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a demand arrives as final, then ask what interest or constraint still needs to be solved.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe a quiet response after pressure; note the risk that may have gone unseen.
ifThenPlans.plan: If silence follows a hard demand, then mark one concern and choose the least risky way to surface it.

ifThenPlans.context: Observe yourself diagnosing personality; note the task problem you can still name.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you start judging the Diminisher's character, then rewrite the sentence as a problem, constraint, or request.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Audit one sent message for 10 minutes. Mark the line where you argued a position; below it, write the interest, constraint, or risk you should have made visible.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, write one if-then trigger for the coming week: if a demand arrives as final, then I will mark the constraint and ask one how-question before I answer.

memorableLines.text: The price of blank compliance is hidden risk with your name still near it.
memorableLines.why: It names the cost of the default quiet response.

memorableLines.text: What can you influence before status eats the facts?
memorableLines.why: It turns control-versus-influence into a pointed question.

memorableLines.text: Keep the problem on the table.
memorableLines.why: It gives the central image a short command.
